claim: A single nuclear gene can be translated into a dual localized protein that distributes between the cytosol and mitochondria.
source: A single nuclear gene can be translated into a dual localized protein that distributes between the cytosol and mitochondria.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the biological phenomenon being studied.

claim: Mitoproteomes contain lots of dual localized proteins termed echoforms.
source: Accumulating evidences show that mitoproteomes contain lots of these dual localized proteins termed echoforms.
evidence: The manuscript states this as an established finding based on accumulating evidence.

claim: The GFP signal of the cytosolic echoform will almost inevitably mask that of the mitochondrial echoform when using current GFP fusion microscopy approaches.
source: Unraveling the existence of mitochondrial echoforms using current GFP (Green Fluorescent Protein) fusion microscopy approaches is extremely difficult because the GFP signal of the cytosolic echoform will almost inevitably mask that of the mitochondrial echoform.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing methods that motivates the development of the new system.

claim: A yeast strain expressing Bi-Genomic Mitochondrial-Split-GFP (BiG Mito-Split-GFP) was engineered.
source: We therefore engineered a yeast strain expressing a new type of Split-GFP that we termed Bi-Genomic Mitochondrial-Split-GFP (BiG Mito-Split-GFP).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental work performed.

claim: In BiG Mito-Split-GFP, one moiety of the GFP is translated from the mitochondrial machinery while the other is fused to the nuclear-encoded protein of interest translated in the cytosol.
source: Because one moiety of the GFP is translated from the mitochondrial machinery while the other is fused to the nuclear-encoded protein of interest translated in the cytosol, the self-reassembly of this Bi-Genomic-encoded Split-GFP is confined to mitochondria.
evidence: This describes the design principle of the BiG Mito-Split-GFP system.

claim: The self-reassembly of Bi-Genomic-encoded Split-GFP is confined to mitochondria.
source: Because one moiety of the GFP is translated from the mitochondrial machinery while the other is fused to the nuclear-encoded protein of interest translated in the cytosol, the self-reassembly of this Bi-Genomic-encoded Split-GFP is confined to mitochondria.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the system design and is stated explicitly.

claim: The BiG Mito-Split-GFP system can authenticate the mitochondrial importability of any protein or echoform from yeast.
source: We could authenticate the mitochondrial importability of any protein or echoform from yeast, but also from other organisms such as the human Argonaute 2 mitochondrial echoform.
evidence: This is stated as a capability demonstrated in the study.

claim: The BiG Mito-Split-GFP system can authenticate the mitochondrial importability of proteins from other organisms such as the human Argonaute 2 mitochondrial echoform.
source: We could authenticate the mitochondrial importability of any protein or echoform from yeast, but also from other organisms such as the human Argonaute 2 mitochondrial echoform.
evidence: This is stated as a demonstrated capability with a specific example.

claim: Mitochondria provide aerobic eukaryotes with adenosine triphosphate (ATP), which involves carbohydrates and fatty acid oxidation.
source: Mitochondria provide aerobic eukaryotes with adenosine triphosphate (ATP), which involves carbohydrates and fatty acid oxidation (Saraste, 1999), as well as numerous other vital functions like lipid and sterol synthesis (Horvath and Daum, 2013) and formation of iron-sulfur cluster (Lill et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Saraste, 1999.

claim: Mitochondria have vital functions including lipid and sterol synthesis.
source: Mitochondria provide aerobic eukaryotes with adenosine triphosphate (ATP), which involves carbohydrates and fatty acid oxidation (Saraste, 1999), as well as numerous other vital functions like lipid and sterol synthesis (Horvath and Daum, 2013) and formation of iron-sulfur cluster (Lill et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Horvath and Daum, 2013.

claim: Mitochondria have vital functions including formation of iron-sulfur cluster.
source: Mitochondria provide aerobic eukaryotes with adenosine triphosphate (ATP), which involves carbohydrates and fatty acid oxidation (Saraste, 1999), as well as numerous other vital functions like lipid and sterol synthesis (Horvath and Daum, 2013) and formation of iron-sulfur cluster (Lill et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lill et al., 2012.

claim: Mitochondria possess their own genome, remnant of an ancestral prokaryotic genome.
source: Mitochondria possess their own genome, remnant of an ancestral prokaryotic genome (Gray, 2017; Margulis, 1975) that has been considerably reduced in size due to a massive transfer of genes during eukaryotic evolution (Thorsness and Weber, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gray, 2017 and Margulis, 1975.

claim: The mitochondrial genome has been considerably reduced in size due to a massive transfer of genes during eukaryotic evolution.
source: Mitochondria possess their own genome, remnant of an ancestral prokaryotic genome (Gray, 2017; Margulis, 1975) that has been considerably reduced in size due to a massive transfer of genes during eukaryotic evolution (Thorsness and Weber, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Thorsness and Weber, 1996.

claim: Most of the proteins required for mitochondrial structure and functions are expressed from the nuclear genome (>99%).
source: As a result, most of the proteins required for mitochondrial structure and functions are expressed from the nuclear genome (>99%) and synthetized as precursors targeted to the mitochondria by mitochondrial targeting signals (MTS), that in some case are cleaved upon import (Chacinska et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chacinska et al., 2009.

claim: Nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins are synthetized as precursors targeted to the mitochondria by mitochondrial targeting signals (MTS), that in some case are cleaved upon import.
source: As a result, most of the proteins required for mitochondrial structure and functions are expressed from the nuclear genome (>99%) and synthetized as precursors targeted to the mitochondria by mitochondrial targeting signals (MTS), that in some case are cleaved upon import (Chacinska et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chacinska et al., 2009.

claim: About a third of the mitochondrial proteins (mitoproteome) in yeast S. cerevisiae have been suggested to be dual localized.
source: In the yeast S. cerevisiae, about a third of the mitochondrial proteins (mitoproteome) have been suggested to be dual localized (Ben-Menachem et al., 2011; Dinur-Mills et al., 2008; Kisslov et al., 2014), and have been named echoforms (or echoproteins) to accentuate the fact that two identical or nearly identical forms of a protein, can reside in the mitochondria and another compartment (Ben-Menachem and Pines, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ben-Menachem et al., 2011; Dinur-Mills et al., 2008; Kisslov et al., 2014.

claim: Dual localized proteins have been named echoforms (or echoproteins) to accentuate the fact that two identical or nearly identical forms of a protein can reside in the mitochondria and another compartment.
source: In the yeast S. cerevisiae, about a third of the mitochondrial proteins (mitoproteome) have been suggested to be dual localized (Ben-Menachem et al., 2011; Dinur-Mills et al., 2008; Kisslov et al., 2014), and have been named echoforms (or echoproteins) to accentuate the fact that two identical or nearly identical forms of a protein, can reside in the mitochondria and another compartment (Ben-Menachem and Pines, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ben-Menachem and Pines, 2017.

claim: Determination of a complete mitoproteome remains challenging due to two coexisting forms and the difficulty to obtain pure mitochondria.
source: Due to these two coexisting forms and the difficulty to obtain pure mitochondria, determination of a complete mitoproteome remains challenging and gave rise to conflicting results (Kumar et al., 2002; Morgenstern et al., 2017; Reinders et al., 2006; Sickmann et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies showing conflicting results.

claim: Engineering green fluorescent protein (GFP) fusions has the major advantage that these fusions can be visualized in living cells using epifluorescence microscopy.
source: Among all possible methods used to identify the subcellular destination of a protein, engineering green fluorescent protein (GFP) fusions has the major advantage that these fusions can be visualized in living cells using epifluorescence microscopy.
evidence: This is stated as an established advantage of GFP fusion technology.

claim: GFP fusion method is suitable to discriminate the cytosolic and mitochondrial pools of dual localized proteins when the cytosolic fraction has a lower concentration than the mitochondrial one.
source: This method is suitable to discriminate the cytosolic and mitochondrial pools of dual localized proteins when the cytosolic fraction has a lower concentration than the mitochondrial one (Weill et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Weill et al., 2018.

claim: When the cytosolic echoform is more abundant than the mitochondrial one, this will inevitably eclipse the mitochondrial fluorescence signal.
source: However, when the cytosolic echoform is more abundant than the mitochondrial one, this will inevitably eclipse the mitochondrial fluorescence signal.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of conventional GFP fusion approaches.

claim: In BiG Mito-Split-GFP, one moiety of the GFP is encoded by the mitochondrial genome, while the other one is fused to the nuclear-encoded protein to be tested.
source: To bypass this drawback, we designed a yeast strain containing a new type of Split-GFP system termed Bi-Genomic Mitochondrial-Split-GFP (BiG Mito-Split-GFP) because one moiety of the GFP is encoded by the mitochondrial genome, while the other one is fused to the nuclear-encoded protein to be tested.
evidence: This describes the design of the BiG Mito-Split-GFP system.

claim: In BiG Mito-Split-GFP, both Split-GFP fragments are translated in separate compartments.
source: By doing so, both Split-GFP fragments are translated in separate compartments and only mitochondrial proteins or echoforms of dual localized proteins trigger GFP reconstitution and can be visualized by fluorescence microscopy of living cells.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the BiG Mito-Split-GFP system.

claim: Only mitochondrial proteins or echoforms of dual localized proteins trigger GFP reconstitution in BiG Mito-Split-GFP and can be visualized by fluorescence microscopy of living cells.
source: By doing so, both Split-GFP fragments are translated in separate compartments and only mitochondrial proteins or echoforms of dual localized proteins trigger GFP reconstitution and can be visualized by fluorescence microscopy of living cells.
evidence: This describes the specificity of the BiG Mito-Split-GFP system.

claim: The BiG Mito-Split-GFP system was validated with proteins exclusively localized in the mitochondria.
source: We herein first validated this system with proteins exclusively localized in the mitochondria and with the dual localized glutamyl-tRNA synthetase (cERS) that resides and functions in both the cytosol and mitochondria as we have shown previously (Frechin et al., 2009; Frechin et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the validation experiments performed.

claim: The dual localized glutamyl-tRNA synthetase (cERS) resides and functions in both the cytosol and mitochondria.
source: We herein first validated this system with proteins exclusively localized in the mitochondria and with the dual localized glutamyl-tRNA synthetase (cERS) that resides and functions in both the cytosol and mitochondria as we have shown previously (Frechin et al., 2009; Frechin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: The BiG Mito-Split-GFP strategy was applied to the near-complete set of all known yeast cytosolic aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases.
source: We next applied our Split-GFP strategy to the near-complete set of all known yeast cytosolic aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases.
evidence: This describes the scope of the screening experiments.

claim: Cytosolic phenylalanyl-tRNA synthetase 2 (cFRS2) has a dual localization.
source: Interestingly, we discovered that two of them, cytosolic phenylalanyl-tRNA synthetase 2 (cFRS2) and cytosolic histidinyl-tRNA synthetase have a dual localization.
evidence: This is stated as a discovery from the screening experiments.

claim: Cytosolic histidinyl-tRNA synthetase has a dual localization.
source: Interestingly, we discovered that two of them, cytosolic phenylalanyl-tRNA synthetase 2 (cFRS2) and cytosolic histidinyl-tRNA synthetase have a dual localization.
evidence: This is stated as a discovery from the screening experiments.

claim: The dual cellular location of cytosolic cysteinyl-tRNA synthetase (cCRS) was recently reported.
source: We also confirmed the recently reported dual cellular location of cytosolic cysteinyl-tRNA synthetase (cCRS) (Nishimura et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nishimura et al., 2019.

claim: The yeast BiG Mito-Split-GFP strain can be used to better define non-conventional mitochondrial targeting sequences.
source: We further demonstrate that our yeast BiG Mito-Split-GFP strain can be used to better define non-conventional mitochondrial targeting sequences and to probe the mitochondrial importability of proteins from other eukaryotic species (human, mouse and plants).
evidence: This is stated as a demonstrated capability of the system.

claim: The yeast BiG Mito-Split-GFP strain can be used to probe the mitochondrial importability of proteins from other eukaryotic species (human, mouse and plants).
source: We further demonstrate that our yeast BiG Mito-Split-GFP strain can be used to better define non-conventional mitochondrial targeting sequences and to probe the mitochondrial importability of proteins from other eukaryotic species (human, mouse and plants).
evidence: This is stated as a demonstrated capability of the system.

claim: The mammalian Argonaute 2 protein heterologously expressed in yeast localizes inside mitochondria.
source: For instance, we show that the mammalian Argonaute 2 protein heterologously expressed in yeast localizes inside mitochondria.
evidence: This is stated as a specific finding from the study.

claim: The scaffold of the self-assembling Superfolder Split-GFP fragments designed by Cabantous and coworkers was used.
source: We used the scaffold of the self-assembling Superfolder Split-GFP fragments designed by Cabantous and coworkers (Cabantous et al., 2005b; Pédelacq et al., 2006), where the 11 beta strands forming active Superfolder GFP are separated in a fragment encompassing the 10 first beta strands (GFPβ1-10) and a smaller one consisting of the remaining beta strand (GFPβ11).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cabantous et al., 2005b and Pédelacq et al., 2006.

claim: The 11 beta strands forming active Superfolder GFP are separated in a fragment encompassing the 10 first beta strands (GFPβ1-10) and a smaller one consisting of the remaining beta strand (GFPβ11).
source: We used the scaffold of the self-assembling Superfolder Split-GFP fragments designed by Cabantous and coworkers (Cabantous et al., 2005b; Pédelacq et al., 2006), where the 11 beta strands forming active Superfolder GFP are separated in a fragment encompassing the 10 first beta strands (GFPβ1-10) and a smaller one consisting of the remaining beta strand (GFPβ11).
evidence: This describes the structure of the Split-GFP system used.

claim: Seven amino acid residues of GFPβ1-10 and three of GFPβ11 were replaced in order to increase the stability and the self-assembly of both fragments.
source: Seven amino acid (aa) residues of GFPβ1-10 and three of GFPβ11 were replaced in order to increase the stability and the self-assembly of both fragments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes modifications made to the Split-GFP fragments, with reference to a figure.

claim: Three β11 strands (GFPβ11-chaplet; β11ch) were concatenated and fused, linked by GTGGGSGGGSTS spacers, to increase the fluorescent signal and facilitate observation of low-abundant proteins.
source: To increase the fluorescent signal and facilitate observation of low-abundant proteins, we concatenated and fused three β11 strands (GFPβ11-chaplet; β11ch) linked by GTGGGSGGGSTS spacers (see Materials and methods for DNA sequence, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, as in Kamiyama et al., 2016; Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes a design feature to enhance signal, with reference to Kamiyama et al., 2016.

claim: The RKY112 strain grew well on respiratory carbon source as wild type yeast (MR6).
source: The RKY112 strain grew well on respiratory carbon source as wild type yeast (MR6) (Figure 1B), produced ATP effectively (Figure 1C), and expressed normally Atp6 and all the other mitochondria-encoded proteins (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The RKY112 strain produced ATP effectively.
source: The RKY112 strain grew well on respiratory carbon source as wild type yeast (MR6) (Figure 1B), produced ATP effectively (Figure 1C), and expressed normally Atp6 and all the other mitochondria-encoded proteins (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The RKY112 strain expressed normally Atp6 and all the other mitochondria-encoded proteins.
source: The RKY112 strain grew well on respiratory carbon source as wild type yeast (MR6) (Figure 1B), produced ATP effectively (Figure 1C), and expressed normally Atp6 and all the other mitochondria-encoded proteins (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Expression of Pam16β11ch resulted in strong GFP signal emissions that colocalized with MitoTracker Red CMXRos-stained mitochondria.
source: Expression of Pam16β11ch and Atp4β11ch resulted in strong GFP signal emissions that colocalized with MitoTracker Red CMXRos-stained mitochondria, whereas no fluorescence was detected with the corresponding empty plasmid (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Expression of Atp4β11ch resulted in strong GFP signal emissions that colocalized with MitoTracker Red CMXRos-stained mitochondria.
source: Expression of Pam16β11ch and Atp4β11ch resulted in strong GFP signal emissions that colocalized with MitoTracker Red CMXRos-stained mitochondria, whereas no fluorescence was detected with the corresponding empty plasmid (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No fluorescence was detected with the empty plasmid in the BiG Mito-Split-GFP strain.
source: Expression of Pam16β11ch and Atp4β11ch resulted in strong GFP signal emissions that colocalized with MitoTracker Red CMXRos-stained mitochondria, whereas no fluorescence was detected with the corresponding empty plasmid (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The GFPβ1-10 polypeptide is well expressed from the mtDNA, stably and correctly folded, allowing reconstitution of an active GFP upon association with the mitochondrial GFPβ11ch-tagged protein.
source: These observations confirmed that the GFPβ1-10 polypeptide is well expressed from the mtDNA, stably and correctly folded, allowing reconstitution of an active GFP upon association with the mitochondrial GFPβ11ch-tagged protein.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations with Pam16β11ch and Atp4β11ch.

claim: Atp4 is present at 30000–40000 copies/cell.
source: So far, the positive controls we used for the proof of concept of the BiG Mito-Split-GFP approach are proteins more or less abundant: Atp4 (30000–40000 copies/cell) and Pam16 (3000 copies/cell) (Morgenstern et al., 2017; Vögtle et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Morgenstern et al., 2017 and Vögtle et al., 2017.

claim: Pam16 is present at 3000 copies/cell.
source: So far, the positive controls we used for the proof of concept of the BiG Mito-Split-GFP approach are proteins more or less abundant: Atp4 (30000–40000 copies/cell) and Pam16 (3000 copies/cell) (Morgenstern et al., 2017; Vögtle et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Morgenstern et al., 2017 and Vögtle et al., 2017.

claim: GatF is a mitochondrial protein that has been reported to be present at only 40–80 copies.
source: This is a mitochondrial protein that has been reported to be present at only 40–80 copies (Vögtle et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vögtle et al., 2017.

claim: Pgk1β11ch and endogenous Pgk1 were well detected by Western blot of total protein extracts probed with anti-Pgk1 antibodies.
source: Pgk1β11ch and endogenous Pgk1 were well detected by Western blot of total protein extracts probed with anti-Pgk1 antibodies (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No GFP fluorescence was observed with Pgk1β11ch.
source: No GFP fluorescence was observed with Pgk1β11ch (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) despite its good expression (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, and Western blot in Figure 2C.

claim: Pgk1 localizes at the external surface of mitochondria.
source: This is an interesting observation considering that Pgk1 localizes at the external surface of mitochondria (Cobine et al., 2004; Kritsiligkou et al., 2017; Levchenko et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cobine et al., 2004; Kritsiligkou et al., 2017; Levchenko et al., 2016.

claim: The BiG Mito-Split-GFP system does not yield any unspecific fluorescence with cytosolic proteins even when they are externally associated to the organelle.
source: This provides the proof that the BiG Mito-Split-GFP system does not yield any unspecific fluorescence with cytosolic proteins even when they are externally associated to the organelle (see also Source data 4).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the Pgk1 negative control experiment.

claim: Any GFPβ11ch-tagged protein that localizes inside the mitochondrial matrix or at matrix side periphery of the inner membrane triggers GFP reconstitution and fluorescence emission.
source: In conclusion, these data show that any GFPβ11ch-tagged protein that localizes inside the mitochondrial matrix or at matrix side periphery of the inner membrane triggers GFP reconstitution and fluorescence emission, making this emission a robust in vivo readout for the mitochondrial importability of proteins of nuclear genetic origin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data with positive and negative controls.

claim: GFP emission in BiG Mito-Split-GFP is a robust in vivo readout for the mitochondrial importability of proteins of nuclear genetic origin.
source: In conclusion, these data show that any GFPβ11ch-tagged protein that localizes inside the mitochondrial matrix or at matrix side periphery of the inner membrane triggers GFP reconstitution and fluorescence emission, making this emission a robust in vivo readout for the mitochondrial importability of proteins of nuclear genetic origin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: cERS is an essential and abundant protein of the cytosolic translation machinery.
source: As we have shown, cERS is an essential and abundant protein of the cytosolic translation machinery, and a small fraction (15%) is located in mitochondria where it is required for mitochondrial protein synthesis and ATP synthase biogenesis (Frechin et al., 2009; Frechin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors (Frechin et al., 2009; Frechin et al., 2014).

claim: A small fraction (15%) of cERS is located in mitochondria where it is required for mitochondrial protein synthesis and ATP synthase biogenesis.
source: As we have shown, cERS is an essential and abundant protein of the cytosolic translation machinery, and a small fraction (15%) is located in mitochondria where it is required for mitochondrial protein synthesis and ATP synthase biogenesis (Frechin et al., 2009; Frechin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors (Frechin et al., 2009; Frechin et al., 2014).

claim: A GFP signal was observed only in mitochondria after transformation of the BiG Mito-Split-GFP strain with plasmids expressing a GFPβ11ch-tagged version of cERS under the control of either the GPD promoter or its own promoter.
source: After transformation of the BiG Mito-Split-GFP strain with plasmids expressing a GFPβ11ch-tagged version of cERS under the control of either the GPD promoter (pGPD) or its own promoter (pGUS1), a GFP signal was observed only in mitochondria (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A stable BiG Mito-Split-GFP strain was generated in which the gene encoding cERSβ11ch was chromosomally expressed under the dependence of its own promoter at the TRP1 locus.
source: We also generated a stable BiG Mito-Split-GFP strain in which the gene encoding cERSβ11ch was chromosomally expressed under the dependence of its own promoter at the TRP1 locus (Supplementary file 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes the construction of a stable strain.

claim: GFP fluorescence was strictly confined to mitochondria in the stable BiG Mito-Split-GFP strain expressing cERSβ11ch from its own promoter.
source: Again, GFP fluorescence was strictly confined to mitochondria (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The BiG Mito-Split-GFP system enables a specific detection in vivo of the mitochondrial pool of cERS (mtecERS), without any interference by the cytosolic echoform.
source: These observations demonstrate that the BiG Mito-Split-GFP system enables a specific detection in vivo of the mitochondrial pool of cERS (mtecERS), without any interference by the cytosolic echoform, which is not possible when cERS is tagged with regular GFP (Frechin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cERS experiments, with reference to previous work.

claim: Detection of the mitochondrial pool of cERS without interference by the cytosolic echoform is not possible when cERS is tagged with regular GFP.
source: These observations demonstrate that the BiG Mito-Split-GFP system enables a specific detection in vivo of the mitochondrial pool of cERS (mtecERS), without any interference by the cytosolic echoform, which is not possible when cERS is tagged with regular GFP (Frechin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Frechin et al., 2009.

claim: Pam16β11ch expression resulted in a specific mitochondrial fluorescence when expressed under the dependence of the GPD promoter at the TRP1 locus.
source: We also expressed Pam16β11ch and Pgk1β11ch under the dependence of the GPD promoter at the TRP1 locus. Again, as shown with the plasmid-borne strategy, Pam16β11ch expression resulted in a specific mitochondrial fluorescence, while Pgk1β11ch gave no fluorescence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pgk1β11ch gave no fluorescence when expressed under the dependence of the GPD promoter at the TRP1 locus.
source: We also expressed Pam16β11ch and Pgk1β11ch under the dependence of the GPD promoter at the TRP1 locus. Again, as shown with the plasmid-borne strategy, Pam16β11ch expression resulted in a specific mitochondrial fluorescence, while Pgk1β11ch gave no fluorescence (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A typical 3D mitochondrial network was reconstituted from the fluorescence induced by the expression of Pam16β11ch, Atp4β11ch and cERSβ11ch in the BiG Mito-Split-GFP strain using high-resolution Airyscan confocal microscopy.
source: Using high-resolution Airyscan confocal microscopy, a typical 3D mitochondrial network was reconstituted from the fluorescence induced by the expression of Pam16β11ch, Atp4β11ch and cERSβ11ch in the BiG Mito-Split-GFP strain whereas, as expected, no fluorescent at all was detected with Pgk1β11ch (Figure 2D), which further illustrates the mitochondrial detection specificity of this system.
evidence: This is supported by 3D reconstruction data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: No fluorescence at all was detected with Pgk1β11ch using high-resolution Airyscan confocal microscopy.
source: Using high-resolution Airyscan confocal microscopy, a typical 3D mitochondrial network was reconstituted from the fluorescence induced by the expression of Pam16β11ch, Atp4β11ch and cERSβ11ch in the BiG Mito-Split-GFP strain whereas, as expected, no fluorescent at all was detected with Pgk1β11ch (Figure 2D), which further illustrates the mitochondrial detection specificity of this system.
evidence: This is supported by 3D reconstruction data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Flow cytometry data corroborated the microscopy observations of the BiG Mito-Split-GFP strain stably expressing Pam16β11ch and Pgk1β11ch.
source: These data were corroborated by flow cytometry analyses of the BiG Mito-Split-GFP strain stably expressing Pam16β11ch and Pgk1β11ch (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Cells co-expressing mtGatFβ1-10 and cERSβ11ch showed a strong and specific mitochondrial fluorescent signal.
source: As expected, a strong and specific mitochondrial fluorescent signal was obtained with cERSβ11ch (Figure 2F, right panel).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Pgk1β11ch resulted in a mitochondrial signal of similar intensity to cERSβ11ch when co-expressed with mtGatFβ1-10.
source: However, Pgk1β11ch resulted in a mitochondrial signal of similar intensity.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the MTS-based Split-GFP control experiment.

claim: The mitochondrial signal with Pgk1β11ch and mtGatFβ1-10 is presumably due to the location at the external surface of mitochondria of a small fraction of the Pgk1 pool that could interact with mtGatFβ1-10 prior to its import into the organelle.
source: This is presumably due to the location at the external surface of mitochondria of a small fraction of the Pgk1 pool that could interact with mtGatFβ1-10 prior to its import into the organelle.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed false positive signal.

claim: The MTS-based strategy can generate a mitochondrial fluorescence without mitochondrial protein internalization due to the high affinity of both self-assembling Split-GFP fragments.
source: These results show that due to the high affinity of both self-assembling Split-GFP fragments, the MTS-based strategy can generate a mitochondrial fluorescence without mitochondrial protein internalization (Figure 2F, right panel).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison experiment shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Compartment-restricted expression of the GFPβ1-10 fragment and GFPβ11ch-tagged proteins increases the reliability of identifying mitochondrial echoforms of dual-localized proteins.
source: These experiments suggest that compartment-restricted expression of the GFPβ1-10 fragment and GFPβ11ch-tagged proteins increases the reliability of identifying mitochondrial echoforms of dual-localized proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of BiG Mito-Split-GFP with MTS-based Split-GFP.

claim: The fraction of cERS which is imported (mtecERS) into mitochondria is essential for the production of mitochondrial Gln-tRNAGln by the transamidation pathway.
source: We showed that the fraction of cERS which is imported (mtecERS) into mitochondria is essential for the production of mitochondrial Gln-tRNAGln by the so-called transamidation pathway (Frechin et al., 2009; Frechin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: In the transamidation pathway, mtecERS aminoacylates the mitochondrial tRNAGln with Glu thereby producing the Glu-tRNAGln that is then converted into Gln-tRNAGln by the GatFAB amidotransferase.
source: In the latter, mtecERS aminoacylates the mitochondrial tRNAGln with Glu thereby producing the Glu-tRNAGln that is then converted into Gln-tRNAGln by the GatFAB amidotransferase (AdT) (Frechin et al., 2009; Frechin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: The results argued against the proposal that mitochondrial import of cQRS compensates for the absence of nuclear-encoded mtQRS in yeast.
source: These results argued against the proposal that mitochondrial import of cQRS compensates for the absence of nuclear-encoded mtQRS in yeast (Rinehart et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the authors' previous work, with reference to Rinehart et al., 2005.

claim: Nothing excludes that cQRS can be imported into mitochondria to fulfill additional tasks beyond translation.
source: This being said, nothing excludes that cQRS can be imported into mitochondria to fulfill additional tasks beyond translation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible functions of cQRS.

claim: S. cerevisiae lacks genes encoding six stricto-senso mtaaRSs: mtARS, mtCRS, mtGRS, mtHRS, mtQRS and mtVRS.
source: Another puzzling concern is the absence in S. cerevisiae of genes encoding six stricto-senso mtaaRSs: mtARS, mtCRS, mtGRS, mtHRS, mtQRS and mtVRS (Table 2).
evidence: This is stated as a known fact with reference to Table 2.

claim: The genes encoding cytosolic equivalents (cytecaaRS) of the missing mtaaRSs might also encode their mitochondrial echoforms (mtecaaRSs).
source: This suggests that the genes encoding their cytosolic equivalents (cytecaaRS) might also encode their mitochondrial echoforms (mtecaaRSs).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the absence of dedicated mitochondrial genes.

claim: Alternative translation/transcription initiation allows the expression of both cytosolic and mitochondrial echoforms for cARS, cGRS1, cHRS, and cVRS.
source: This has been confirmed for cARS, cGRS1, cHRS, cVRS for which alternative translation/transcription initiation allows the expression of both echoforms (Figure 3D; Chang and Wang, 2004; Chatton et al., 1988; Chen et al., 2012; Natsoulis et al., 1986; Turner et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and reference to Figure 3D.

claim: 18 out of the 20 yeast caaRSs were successfully expressed in the BiG Mito-Split-GFP strain.
source: We successfully expressed in the BiG Mito-Split-GFP strain the full length GFPβ11ch-tagged versions of 18 out of 20 yeast caaRSs or cyteaaRSs (Figure 3A–C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Supplementary files 3 and 4).
evidence: This describes the scope of the screening experiments.

claim: The authors failed to obtain the full-length GFPβ11ch-tagged versions of cCRS and cPRS despite repeated attempts.
source: For unknown reasons, we failed to obtain the full-length GFPβ11ch-tagged versions of cCRS and cPRS despite repeated attempts, but successfully cloned the first hundred N-terminal aa residues of cCRS (N100cCRS) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This describes a technical limitation encountered in the study.

claim: An unambiguous mitochondrial fluorescent signal was observed with cFRS2β11ch.
source: An unambiguous mitochondrial fluorescent signal was observed with cFRS2β11ch (the α-subunit of the α2β2 cFRS), cytecHRSβ11ch and N100cCRSβ11ch (Figure 3A–C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: An unambiguous mitochondrial fluorescent signal was observed with cytecHRSβ11ch.
source: An unambiguous mitochondrial fluorescent signal was observed with cFRS2β11ch (the α-subunit of the α2β2 cFRS), cytecHRSβ11ch and N100cCRSβ11ch (Figure 3A–C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: An unambiguous mitochondrial fluorescent signal was observed with N100cCRSβ11ch.
source: An unambiguous mitochondrial fluorescent signal was observed with cFRS2β11ch (the α-subunit of the α2β2 cFRS), cytecHRSβ11ch and N100cCRSβ11ch (Figure 3A–C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The existence of a fully functional mtFRS has been demonstrated.
source: Since the existence of a fully functional mtFRS has been demonstrated (Koerner et al., 1987), it is possible that supernumerary mtecFRS2 we identified is not necessary for charging mitochondrial tRNAPhe but exerts some non-canonical functions, in addition to its role in cytosolic protein synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Koerner et al., 1987.

claim: Supernumerary mtecFRS2 is possibly not necessary for charging mitochondrial tRNAPhe but exerts some non-canonical functions, in addition to its role in cytosolic protein synthesis.
source: Since the existence of a fully functional mtFRS has been demonstrated (Koerner et al., 1987), it is possible that supernumerary mtecFRS2 we identified is not necessary for charging mitochondrial tRNAPhe but exerts some non-canonical functions, in addition to its role in cytosolic protein synthesis.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the finding.

claim: The mitochondrial fluorescence triggered by expression of N100cCRSβ11ch suggests that this part of cCRS harbors a MTS.
source: The mitochondrial fluorescence triggered by expression of N100cCRSβ11ch suggests that this part of cCRS harbors a MTS, which has recently been proposed (Nishimura et al., 2019, see Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data, with reference to Nishimura et al., 2019.

claim: The most plausible hypothesis for cytecHRSβ11ch mitochondrial fluorescence is that the MTS of the mtecHRS is longer than the one originally characterized.
source: The mitochondrial fluorescence triggered by cytecHRSβ11ch is more intriguing. The most plausible hypothesis is that the MTS of the mtecHRS is longer than the one originally characterized.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed fluorescence.

claim: There is possibly a second mitochondrial echoform of cHRS imported inside mitochondria through a cryptic MTS that has yet to be identified.
source: The other possibility is that there is indeed a second mitochondrial echoform of cHRS imported inside mitochondria through a cryptic MTS that has yet to be identified and, like for cFRS2, this new mtecHRS would then most probably exert a non-canonical function.
evidence: This is an alternative speculative explanation.

claim: A mitochondrial GFP staining was observed with mtecARSβ11ch, mtecGRS1β11ch, mtecHRSβ11ch and mtecVRSβ11ch when expressed in the BiG Mito-Split-GFP strain.
source: When mtecARSβ11ch, mtecGRS1β11ch, mtecHRSβ11ch and mtecVRSβ11ch (echoforms that start with the most upstream methionine initiator codon, Figure 3D) were expressed in the BiG Mito-Split-GFP strain, a mitochondrial GFP staining was, as expected, observed with these four mtecaaRSs (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: cytecARSβ11ch, cytecGRS1β11ch and cytecVRSβ11ch (versions without their MTS) did not produce any detectable GFP signal.
source: Conversely, cytecARSβ11ch, cytecGRS1β11ch and cytecVRSβ11ch, versions without their MTS) did not produce any detectable GFP signal confirming the MTS-dependency of these cytosolic echoforms for mitochondria localization (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The lack of GFP signal with cytecARSβ11ch, cytecGRS1β11ch and cytecVRSβ11ch confirms the MTS-dependency of these cytosolic echoforms for mitochondria localization.
source: Conversely, cytecARSβ11ch, cytecGRS1β11ch and cytecVRSβ11ch, versions without their MTS) did not produce any detectable GFP signal confirming the MTS-dependency of these cytosolic echoforms for mitochondria localization (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the negative control experiments.

claim: mtecERS does not involve any processing upon import into mitochondria.
source: Unlike proteins with a MTS that is cleaved upon import into mitochondria, mtecERS does not involve any processing (Frechin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Frechin et al., 2009.

claim: The mitochondrial targeting residues of cERS are presumably located in the N-terminal region.
source: Presumably, the mitochondrial targeting residues are located in the N-terminal (N-ter) region of cERS as in precursors of mitochondrial proteins destined to the matrix.
evidence: This is an inference based on typical MTS locations.

claim: All three N-terminal peptides of cERS (cERSβ11ch-N1, cERSβ11ch-N2, and cERSβ11ch-N3) produced a GFP fluorescence signal that matched the labeling of mitochondria with MitoTracker Red CMXRos.
source: All three peptides produced a GFP fluorescence signal that matched the labeling of mitochondria with MitoTracker Red CMXRos (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: No GFP fluorescence was detected with cERSβ11ch lacking the residues 1–30 or 1–200 (cERSβ11ch-∆N1 and cERSβ11ch-∆N2 respectively).
source: Consistently, no GFP fluorescence was detected with cERSβ11ch lacking the residues 1–30 or 1–200 (cERSβ11ch-∆N1 and cERSβ11ch-∆N2 respectively) (Figure 4B) despite detection by WB of these truncated proteins in cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data in Figure 4B and Western blot in Figure 4C.

claim: cERS' MTS is narrowed down to the 30 first aa residues of its N-ter domain.
source: These data narrow down cERS' MTS to the 30 first aa residues of its N-ter domain; this segment is made of a short β-strand and a 13 aa long α-chain (Simader et al., 2006) likely harboring the import signal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the deletion analysis, with reference to structural data.

claim: The N-terminal 30 residues of cERS are made of a short β-strand and a 13 aa long α-chain likely harboring the import signal.
source: These data narrow down cERS' MTS to the 30 first aa residues of its N-ter domain; this segment is made of a short β-strand and a 13 aa long α-chain (Simader et al., 2006) likely harboring the import signal.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Simader et al., 2006.

claim: Modifying the mitochondrial genome is only possible in S. cerevisiae and Chlamydomonas reinhardtii.
source: The BiG Mito-Split-GFP system is based on modifications in the mitochondrial genome for expressing the GFPβ1-10 fragment inside the organelle. Modifying the mitochondrial genome is thus far only possible in S. cerevisiae and Chlamydomonas reinhardtii (Remacle et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Remacle et al., 2006.

claim: There is a high degree of conservation of mitochondrial protein import systems.
source: Owing to the high degree of conservation of mitochondrial protein import systems (Lithgow and Schneider, 2010), we used the yeast BiG Mito-Split-GFP strain to test the mitochondrial importability of proteins from various eukaryotic origins.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lithgow and Schneider, 2010.

claim: AthcERS is predicted to be a cytosolic protein with a putative chloroplastic targeting signal according to TargetP1.1.
source: According to independent MTS prediction tools, AthcERS would be a cytosolic protein with a putative chloroplastic targeting signal (TargetP1.1), whereas Athmt/chlERS is strongly predicted to be located in mitochondria and chloroplast (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Athmt/chlERS is strongly predicted to be located in mitochondria and chloroplast.
source: According to independent MTS prediction tools, AthcERS would be a cytosolic protein with a putative chloroplastic targeting signal (TargetP1.1), whereas Athmt/chlERS is strongly predicted to be located in mitochondria and chloroplast (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Expression of AthcERS and Athmt/chlERS proteins was confirmed by Western blot.
source: Expression of these proteins was confirmed by Western blot (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: AthcERSβ11ch did not produce any GFP signal.
source: AthcERSβ11ch did not produce any GFP signal, whereas consistent with its predicted localization Athmt/chlERSβ11ch resulted in a specific mitochondrial fluorescence staining (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Athmt/chlERSβ11ch resulted in a specific mitochondrial fluorescence staining, consistent with its predicted localization.
source: AthcERSβ11ch did not produce any GFP signal, whereas consistent with its predicted localization Athmt/chlERSβ11ch resulted in a specific mitochondrial fluorescence staining (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The yeast BiG Mito-Split-GFP system can be used to analyze mitochondrial localization of plant proteins.
source: These data show that the yeast BiG Mito-Split-GFP system can be used to analyze mitochondrial localization of plant proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Arabidopsis ERS experiments.

claim: Ago2 mainly localizes to the nucleoplasm and cell junctions where it is required for RNA-mediated gene silencing (RNAi) by the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC).
source: This protein mainly localizes to the nucleoplasm and cell junctions where it is required for RNA-mediated gene silencing (RNAi) by the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) (Hammond et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hammond et al., 2000.

claim: In some studies, Ago2 was suggested to be associated to mitochondria, but it remains unclear whether it localizes at the external surface or inside the organelle.
source: In some studies, Ago2 was suggested to be associated to mitochondria, but it remains unclear whether it localizes at the external surface or inside the organelle (Barrey et al., 2011; Shepherd et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barrey et al., 2011 and Shepherd et al., 2017.

claim: A potential MTS could not be predicted in Ago2 proteins from human, mouse, Bos taurus, Danio rerio and Drosophila melanogaster using four different algorithms.
source: Using four different algorithms a potential MTS could not be predicted in Ago2 proteins from human, mouse, Bos taurus, Danio rerio andDrosophila melanogaster, casting doubts on the mitochondrial import of Ago2 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Expression of MmuAgo2β11ch and HsaAgo2β11ch was confirmed by Western blot.
source: Expression of each of these GFPβ11ch-tagged constructs was confirmed by WB, and both generated a solid and specific GFP fluorescence restricted to mitochondria (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: Both MmuAgo2β11ch and HsaAgo2β11ch generated a solid and specific GFP fluorescence restricted to mitochondria.
source: Expression of each of these GFPβ11ch-tagged constructs was confirmed by WB, and both generated a solid and specific GFP fluorescence restricted to mitochondria (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: The observations provide strong evidence that in addition to a cytosolic and nuclear location, Ago2 is also transported into mitochondria and is really a multi-localized protein with a mitochondrial echoform.
source: These observations provide strong evidence that in addition to a cytosolic and nuclear location, Ago2 is also transported into mitochondria and is really a multi-localized protein with a mitochondrial echoform.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Ago2 experiments.

claim: The Split-GFP technology was initially designed to study protein-protein interactions and solubility.
source: Initially designed to study protein-protein interactions and solubility, the Split-GFP technology was almost immediately hijacked to track protein localization in various cell types and compartments (Hyun et al., 2015; Kaddoum et al., 2010; Kamiyama et al., 2016; Külzer et al., 2013; Pinaud and Dahan, 2011; Van Engelenburg and Palmer, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing the evolution of Split-GFP applications.

claim: Split-GFP has been used to study the mitochondrial localization of PARK7 upon nutrient starvation.
source: It has also been used to study the mitochondrial localization of PARK7 upon nutrient starvation (Calì et al., 2015), and to detect remodeling of MERCs (mitochondria-ER contact sites) in mammalian cells (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Calì et al., 2015.

claim: Split-GFP has been used to detect remodeling of MERCs (mitochondria-ER contact sites) in mammalian cells.
source: It has also been used to study the mitochondrial localization of PARK7 upon nutrient starvation (Calì et al., 2015), and to detect remodeling of MERCs (mitochondria-ER contact sites) in mammalian cells (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2018.

claim: Kakimoto and coworkers developed in yeast and mammalian cells a Split-based system to analyze inter-organelles contact sites.
source: Recently, Kakimoto and coworkers developed in yeast and mammalian cells a Split-based system to analyze inter-organelles contact sites (Kakimoto et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kakimoto et al., 2018.

claim: In previous Split-GFP approaches, both GFPβ1-10 and GFPβ11 were anchored to proteins either translated in the cytosol or following the secretory pathway.
source: However, in these approaches both GFPβ1-10 and GFPβ11 were anchored to proteins either translated in the cytosol or following the secretory pathway.
evidence: This describes a limitation of previous Split-GFP approaches.

claim: The simultaneous synthesis of both GFP fragments in the cytosol, coupled to their high affinity to self-assemble, may induce potential false-positive GFP emission.
source: Although the latter may avoid nonspecific interaction or reconstitution of the two GFP parts, we bring herein proofs that the simultaneous synthesis of both fragments in the cytosol, coupled to their high affinity to self-assemble, may induce potential false-positive GFP emission (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: In the BiG Mito-Split-GFP system, the first 10 segments of beta barrel GFP (GFPβ1-10) is expressed from the mitochondrial genome and translated inside the organelle without interfering with mitochondrial function.
source: To bypass this issue, we describe herein a new and robust Split-GFP system where the first 10 segments of beta barrel GFP (GFPβ1-10) is expressed from the mitochondrial genome and translated inside the organelle without interfering with mitochondrial function (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Any detected GFP fluorescence in BiG Mito-Split-GFP obligatorily originates from the organelle thereby demonstrating a mitochondrial localization for the tested proteins.
source: As a result, any detected GFP fluorescence obligatory originates from the organelle thereby demonstrating a mitochondrial localization for the tested proteins (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This is a conclusion about the specificity of the system, with reference to Figure 6A–B.

claim: The BiG Mito-Split-GFP system was successfully tested with two mitochondrial proteins (Atp4 and Pam16), and a cytosolic one (Pgk1) as a negative control.
source: This system was first successfully tested with two mitochondrial proteins (Atp4 and Pam16), and a cytosolic one (Pgk1) as a negative control.
evidence: This summarizes the validation experiments.

claim: The mitochondrial echoform of the cytosolic glutamyl-tRNA synthetase (mtecERS) encoded by the GUS1 nuclear gene was detected with the BiG Mito-Split-GFP system.
source: Moreover, the mitochondrial echoform of the cytosolic glutamyl-tRNA synthetase (mtecERS) encoded by the GUS1 nuclear gene was also detected with the BiG Mito-Split-GFP system (Figures 2, 3, 4 and 6A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2, 3, 4 and 6A.

claim: Synchronous release of cERS and cMRS from the cytosolic anchor Arc1 protein is required for a coordinated expression of mitochondrial and nuclear ATP synthase genes.
source: As we already showed, synchronous release of cERS and cMRS from the cytosolic anchor Arc1 protein is required for a coordinated expression of mitochondrial and nuclear ATP synthase genes (Frechin et al., 2009; Frechin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Mitochondrial relocation of cERS is consistent with the functional plasticity of caaRSs with multiple locations in cells.
source: Mitochondrial relocation of cERS is consistent with the functional plasticity of caaRSs with multiple locations in cells.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the specific finding to a broader concept.

claim: The BiG Mito-Split-GFP system allows to visualize in living cells the mitochondrial pool of proteins with multiple cellular locations.
source: These findings demonstrate that the BiG Mito-Split-GFP system allows not only to visualize in living cells the mitochondrial pool of proteins with multiple cellular locations, but also to decipher their non-conventional MTSs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cERS MTS mapping experiments.

claim: The BiG Mito-Split-GFP system allows to decipher non-conventional MTSs of proteins with multiple cellular locations.
source: These findings demonstrate that the BiG Mito-Split-GFP system allows not only to visualize in living cells the mitochondrial pool of proteins with multiple cellular locations, but also to decipher their non-conventional MTSs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cERS MTS mapping experiments.

claim: Recent efforts to identify mitochondrial proteins and assign their submitochondrial localization revealed an exquisite precision.
source: Recent efforts made to identify mitochondrial proteins and assign their submitochondrial localization revealed an exquisite precision (Morgenstern et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Morgenstern et al., 2017.

claim: Resolving mitochondrial proteomes is challenging due to the difficulty of obtaining pure mitochondria and because many proteins transiently localize in mitochondria and are found elsewhere in cells.
source: However, resolving mitochondrial proteomes is challenging due to the difficulty of obtaining pure mitochondria and because many proteins transiently localize in mitochondria and are found elsewhere in cells.
evidence: This describes ongoing challenges in the field.

claim: Up to 10–20% of the yeast mitoproteome was suggested to be composed of proteins with another location in cells.
source: Up to 10–20% of the yeast mitoproteome was suggested to be composed of proteins with another location in cells (i.e the cytosol, the nucleus, ER…) (Ben-Menachem and Pines, 2017; Morgenstern et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ben-Menachem and Pines, 2017 and Morgenstern et al., 2017.

claim: The BiG Mito-Split-GFP system will be especially helpful to resolve mitochondrial proteome complexities.
source: Our BiG Mito-Split-GFP system will be especially helpful to resolve these proteome complexities.
evidence: This is a prospective statement about the utility of the system.

claim: Some aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases are well-known to relocate in different compartments to fulfill a wide range of cellular activities.
source: This system was here applied to proteins involved in tRNA aminoacylation, some of which are well-known to relocate in different compartment to fulfill a wide range of cellular activities (Han et al., 2012; Ko et al., 2000; Yakobov et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Han et al., 2012; Ko et al., 2000; Yakobov et al., 2018.

claim: The findings provide strong evidence that cFRS2 and cytecHRS are dual localized as was observed for cERS.
source: In this way, we provide strong evidence that cFRS2 and cytecHRS are dual localized as was observed for cERS, which suggests that these proteins may have additional roles beyond translation (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the screening experiments, with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: cFRS2 and cytecHRS may have additional roles beyond translation.
source: In this way, we provide strong evidence that cFRS2 and cytecHRS are dual localized as was observed for cERS, which suggests that these proteins may have additional roles beyond translation (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a speculative inference from the dual localization finding.

claim: Being dually localized in the cytosol and mitochondria, and since there is no mtecFRS1, it can be inferred that the catalytic α-subunit (cFRS2) is not inevitably in complex with the β-subunit within the α2β2 heterotetrameric form of cFRS.
source: Being dually localized in the cytosol and mitochondria, and since there is no mtecFRS1, it can be inferred that the catalytic α-subunit (cFRS2) is not inevitably in complex with the β-subunit within the α2β2 heterotetrameric form of cFRS.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the dual localization of cFRS2.

claim: A bona fide mtFRS (encoded by the MSF1 gene) that functions as a monomer is essential to generate mitochondrial Phe-tRNAPhe in mitochondria.
source: A bona fide mtFRS (encoded by the MSF1 gene) that was shown to function as a monomer is essential to generate mitochondrial Phe-tRNAPhe (F-mttRNAF) in mitochondria (Sanni et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sanni et al., 1991.

claim: mtecFRS2 is likely not required to produce F-mttRNAF but more likely has a non-canonical yet-to-be-discovered function.
source: This further supports the hypothesis that mtecFRS2 is not required to produce F-mttRNAF but more likely has a non-canonical yet-to-be-discovered function.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the existence of mtFRS.

claim: The failure to detect a mitochondrial echoform for cQRS is consistent with previous findings that the only source of Q-mttRNAQ in mitochondria is provided by the relocation of mtecERS into the organelle.
source: Our failure to detect a mitochondrial echoform for cQRS is consistent with our previous findings (Frechin et al., 2009) that the only source of Q-mttRNAQ in mitochondria is provided by the relocation of mtecERS into the organelle (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) de concert with the tRNA-dependent GatFAB Adt (Frechin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The findings definitely cast in doubt the previous proposal of the existence of a cQRS mitochondrial echoform.
source: This definitely casts in doubt the previous proposal of the existence of a cQRS mitochondrial echoform (Rinehart et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a conclusion that contradicts a previous proposal, with reference to Rinehart et al., 2005.

claim: Mitochondrial echoforms of cCRS result from alternative transcription and translation starts.
source: In agreement with our results (Figure 3C), mitochondrial echoforms of cCRS were also detected in a recent study and shown to result from alternative transcription and translation starts (Nishimura et al., 2019), thereby unraveling how mtCRS is expressed from the CRS1 gene and rationalizing how mitochondrial Cys-tRNACys is produced.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nishimura et al., 2019 and data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No specific motif was found in the N-terminal regions of newly identified mitochondrial echoforms of caaRSs using MAST/MEME analysis.
source: Having identified new mitochondrial echoforms of caaRSs, we wondered if they carry in their N-terminal regions some common specific sequence or structural features possibly driving mitochondrial import. No specific motif was found using MAST/MEME analysis (Bailey et al., 2009), and there was no significant sequence similarity (as tested with Blast) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis, with reference to Bailey et al., 2009.

claim: There was no significant sequence similarity in the N-terminal regions of newly identified mitochondrial echoforms of caaRSs as tested with Blast.
source: Having identified new mitochondrial echoforms of caaRSs, we wondered if they carry in their N-terminal regions some common specific sequence or structural features possibly driving mitochondrial import. No specific motif was found using MAST/MEME analysis (Bailey et al., 2009), and there was no significant sequence similarity (as tested with Blast) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: All but mtecARS show at least one α−helix within their 50 first aa residues.
source: All but mtecARS show at least one α−helix within their 50 first aa residues, and most (except cERS) are enriched in positively- vs negatively-charged aa residues, as in classical mitochondrial targeting sequences.
evidence: This is an observation from structural analysis.

claim: Most of the newly identified mitochondrial echoforms of caaRSs (except cERS) are enriched in positively- vs negatively-charged aa residues, as in classical mitochondrial targeting sequences.
source: All but mtecARS show at least one α−helix within their 50 first aa residues, and most (except cERS) are enriched in positively- vs negatively-charged aa residues, as in classical mitochondrial targeting sequences.
evidence: This is an observation from sequence analysis.

claim: Most of the cytosolic form of cERS interacts with Arc1 in fermenting yeast.
source: As we have shown, most of the cytosolic form of cERS interacts with Arc1 in fermenting yeast, but during the diauxic shift, Arc1 expression is repressed, allowing the generation of a free pool of cERS able to relocate into mitochondria.
evidence: This is stated as a previously shown finding.

claim: During the diauxic shift, Arc1 expression is repressed, allowing the generation of a free pool of cERS able to relocate into mitochondria.
source: As we have shown, most of the cytosolic form of cERS interacts with Arc1 in fermenting yeast, but during the diauxic shift, Arc1 expression is repressed, allowing the generation of a free pool of cERS able to relocate into mitochondria.
evidence: This is stated as a previously shown finding.

claim: In the case of cERS, interactions of its N-terminal domain seem to be important to distribute it between the cytosol and mitochondria.
source: Thus, in the case of this caaRS, interactions of its N-terminal domain seem to be important to distribute it between the cytosol and mitochondria.
evidence: This is an inference from the Arc1 interaction mechanism.

claim: The yeast BiG Mito-Split-GFP system is robust, not expensive and can be used to test proteins from various organisms.
source: The yeast BiG Mito-Split-GFP system we describe here is designed to point out mitochondrial echoforms. It is robust, not expensive and can be used to test proteins from various organisms.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the system's characteristics.

claim: The BiG Mito-Split-GFP system has many potential applications and opens new avenues in the study of mitochondria and their communications with other compartments of the cell.
source: This new approach has certainly many potential applications and opens new avenues in the study of mitochondria and their communications with other compartments of the cell.
evidence: This is a prospective statement about future applications.
